title: Heart Sutra, Part 5: Making Friends with Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing the interconnectedness and impermanence of life, recognizing that our concepts and words cannot fully capture reality. This understanding, known as "emptiness," allows us to approach experience with a more open and receptive mindset, cultivating flexibility, acceptance, and love in our relationships with others. By letting go of our need for fixed identities and separate selves, we can develop a deeper appreciation for the fluid and dynamic nature of life, leading to greater freedom and connection.

The heart of our practice, the heart of our lives, and central to the strange little chant is the odd term, strange odd, why did I come to this place?
Emptiness, emptiness, which is a wonderful thing and a little baffling at first and later on too.
But incredibly helpful, like life changing, as we live into it.
It's hard to understand, and maybe it's safe to say that it's impossible to understand if we think about the word "understand" the way we usually think about it.
To understand something seems to mean that we shift our collection of concepts and ideas around so that the new thing fits in.
Which might mean we need to rearrange our existing collection of ideas and concepts.
Or maybe we just tweak to our own devising whatever the new thing is.
We do that too, right?
Because we want the world to make sense and we want us to make sense.
But emptiness is exactly about the way the world can't be contained and defined by our concepts and words.
That there's something much vaster, more mysterious, more interconnected and interpenetrating.
And when we have words for these things, I'm using words, and yet somehow beyond even those words.
So maybe we need a different word from "understanding" in our studies of this pointer to a concept about non-concepts, which is emptiness.
The word "appreciate" is often used.
I think that's a good word.
Can we appreciate emptiness more deeply?
Can we appreciate our lives more deeply?
Sometimes we study a Japanese teacher who's seen as the founder of this school from the 13th century named Dogen.
His writing is all laced with this, laced with emptiness, and it's really hard to understand in that way.

All right.

All right.
Okay.

So I think it's a gradual process too.

You learn something new or you have an experience in life.

I think when that's happening, I'm more open and more accepting, more flexible.

More in accord with emptiness, more open.

And how is it we ever get along?

So I was trying to think about what happens in detail in these two states in regard to the five skandhas.
And if you weren't here for those talks, and in general, it might be useful to have the Heart Sutra open in the chant book on page whatever it is.
We're so precise now.
Yeah, we know all the pages now.
Amazing.
I was thinking how precise it was that I sat down: now's the time to do this.
Now, page two, now this.
It's great.
We know what we're doing.
Anyway, early on the text talks about these five categories of experience called aggregates or skandhas.

But we were reviewing at some length the other week that this teaching is really useful with or without emptiness.
Emptiness just makes it even better.

The Buddha said one of the ways to loosen up your self-referential, self-centered self, which we are in love with and in hate with all at the same time, and all kinds of relationship with, is to actually take a fresh look at experience.
And you may see that all your experience can't exactly be explained by me or me-ness.
But maybe it could be explained by these five categories, as he gives these five categories.
So I was thinking about when I'm closed and reactive with the five skandhas.
The first of them is form, physicality, and how it feels in the body to feel constricted, annoyed, icky, right?
So you can notice that.
And then already the conversation is starting to change, right?

I don't think a lot about perception when I'm constricted and reactive, except when it starts to shift, especially when the reactivity starts to lift.
And then that's one of the first things I notice: "Oh, my perspective shifted a little bit there.
Look at that."
And so those Buddhist teachings are saying, is that you figuring it out or is that your perspective shifting, which isn't exactly you, it's perspective.

Yeah, well, impatience arising, but that's justified, right?

So this quality of emptiness, or the aspect of interdependence that it points to (we'll get to that), sometimes called the absolute or the ultimate reality, is the space in which we see none of this stuff is real, not even kind of.

In which that healing happens.
